problems.title: Astrophotography
problems.statement: An astrophotographer, based on the Equator, uses a good digital camera on a tripod, but with no tracking. The camera has a telescopic lens with focal length of 150 mm and aperture (objective diameter) of 84 mm. The sensor has an effective light collecting diameter of 22.5 mm. The photographic target is a star field at the observer’s Zenith.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Calculate the field of view (the angular width of the image) which can be captured on the sensor using this equipment. Give the answer in degrees.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: The pixels in the camera’s sensor are separated by a distance of $3.23\ \mu\mathrm m$. What is the maximum possible exposure time for a single frame, so that no star trails appear on the exposed image? Give the answer in seconds.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: For a better-quality image of the star field, the photographer decides to take multiple shots at the exposure time calculated in b) and then to stack them together. The total time for all these shots is 30 seconds (ignore any time taken to write data to the memory card). What fraction of the total field of view is always visible throughout the shots? Give the answer as a number between 0 and 1.

solution.statement:
**(a)** By simple right angle triangle,

$$\mathrm{FOV}=2\times\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\text{sensor width}}{2\times\text{Focal Length}}\right)=2\times\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{22.5}{2\times150}\right),$$

$$\alpha\approx8.58^\circ.\qquad[2.0]$$

**(b)** Number of pixels on the sensor will be given by,

$$N=\frac{\text{Sensor width}}{\text{pixel width}}=\frac{22.5}{3.23\times10^{-3}}=6965.94.\qquad[1.0]$$

As the number of pixels have to be integer, we take $N=6966$. **[1.0]** Angular coverage of each pixel will be,

$$\text{Pixel view}=\frac{8.578^\circ}{6966}=0.00123^\circ/\text{pixel}\approx4.43''/\text{pixel}.\qquad[1.0]$$

As the stars complete one full circle in 23.9344 hours, **[1.0]**

**Marking note:** student loses this one mark if $15^\circ$ per hour is used.

$$t_1=1.23\times10^{-3}\frac{23.9344^{\mathrm h}}{360}=0.294\ \mathrm s\approx0.3\ \mathrm s.\qquad[1.0]$$

(in reality this is probably a factor of 10 smaller than the eye would detect)

**(c)** In 30 seconds, the sky will move by,

$$\Delta\alpha=\frac{360^\circ}{23.9344\times120}=0.125342^\circ.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\therefore\frac{\alpha-\Delta\alpha}{\alpha}=\frac{8.578-0.125342}{8.578}=98.5\%.\qquad[2.0]$$

(or $8.453^\circ$ is total field of view in high resolution images from the stack)

**Marking note:** Only penalise $15^\circ/\mathrm{hr}$ once in the whole solution.

> **Source note:** The English key’s reprinted part (c) asks “What proportion of the total field of view is possible at the higher signal to noise ratio?”, while the primary bilingual question asks the fraction always visible and specifies a number between 0 and 1. The key prints 98.5%. Its exposure-time line prints hours in the numerator and seconds in the result without an explicit hour-to-second conversion. Both printed forms and both marking notes are retained.

difficulty.rationale: Compute sensor field, sidereal motion per pixel and common stacked area.

problems.title: Flat Earth
problems.statement:
A new model of the world is gaining in popularity among some people. These people believe in the “Flat Earth” view of the world, where the Earth is not a spheroid, but rather a circle with radius $R_\oplus$. The central axis of the Earth (normal to the circle passing through its centre $C$) passes through the observer’s zenith.

This model must at least remain consistent with the observed phenomena, as listed below:

- The value of the solar constant is $S_\oplus=1366\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$.
- The Earth’s central axis precesses in a circle with a period 25800 years.
- The radius of the precession circle is $23.5^\circ$.

Assume that (1) the Earth is a perfect blackbody radiator with uniform temperature and the Sun is sufficiently far away such that all solar rays are parallel and (2) the Sun’s current (initial) location is at the zenith.

Determine how many years it will take for the Earth’s equilibrium temperature to decrease by $1\ ^\circ\mathrm C$.

solution.statement:
Assume the surface area of one side of the flat Earth is $A$. Let the angle between the Sun and the flat Earth’s center axis be $\theta$, where $\theta$ is initially $0^\circ$. As the Sun’s rays are parallel, the power delivered to the Earth by the Sun will be $S_\odot A\cos\theta$ at any given point in time.

At equilibrium, this is the energy radiated away via blackbody radiation, so the equilibrium temperature $T$ satisfies

$$S_\odot A\cos\theta=\sigma(2A)T^4.\qquad[2.0]$$

The factor of 2 comes from the fact that the flat Earth would radiate energy from both sides. This yields

$$T(\theta)=\sqrt[4]{\frac{S_\odot\cos\theta}{2\sigma}},$$

and we wish to find the value of $\theta_1$ such that $T(\theta_1)=T(0)-\Delta T$. Thus,

$$\sqrt[4]{\frac{S_\odot\cos\theta_1}{2\sigma}}=\sqrt[4]{\frac{S_\odot}{2\sigma}}-\Delta T.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$\cos\theta_1=\left(1-\Delta T\sqrt[4]{\frac{2\sigma}{S_\odot}}\right)^4.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\left(1-\sqrt[4]{\frac{2\times5.67\times10^{-8}}{1366}}\right)^4,$$

$$\cos\theta_1=0.9880.\qquad[1.0]$$

Now, we find the time it takes for the axis to make such an angle with the Sun. On the celestial sphere, let $O$ be the center of precession, $Z$ be the current direction of the axis, and $X$ be direction of the axis when it makes an angle of $\theta_1$ with the sun, so $\angle ZCX=\theta_1$. If $\epsilon$ is the radius of precession, then $\angle OCZ=\angle OCX=\epsilon$. **[1.0]**

By the spherical Law of Cosines on angle $O$ of spherical triangle $OXZ$, we have

$$\cos\theta_1=\cos\epsilon\cos\epsilon+\sin\epsilon\sin\epsilon\cos(\widehat O)=\cos^2\epsilon+\sin^2\epsilon\cos(\widehat O),$$

$$\widehat O=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos\theta_1-\cos^2\epsilon}{\sin^2\epsilon}\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\therefore\Delta t=\frac{\widehat O}{2\pi}\times P=\frac{P}{2\pi}\times\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos\theta_1-\cos^2\epsilon}{\sin^2\epsilon}\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\frac{25800}{2\pi}\times\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{0.9880-\cos^2 23.5^\circ}{\sin^2 23.5^\circ}\right)\approx1606\ \mathrm{yr}.$$

Thus, the average temperature of the earth will go down by $1\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ in **just over 1600 years**. **[1.0]**

> **Source note:** The primary question denotes the solar constant $S_\oplus$, while the English key’s reprint and derivation use $S_\odot$. The value is 1366 W/m² in both editions.

problems.title: Mirror
problems.statement: A bored cosmologist comes up with a thought experiment to determine the Hubble constant ($H_0$) for his model of a Steady-State-Universe. In this experiment, a large, fully reflecting flat mirror — carrying several gyroscopes that would maintain its spatial orientation in the same plane — would be placed at a distance $D$ from the Solar System in a region without gravitational influences. From the Earth, a laser beam would be directed towards that region for a long period of time. After a time $T$, the radiation would return and be detected, allowing the determination of the fixed constant $H_0$.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Find an expression for $H_0$ as a function of $D$, $c$ (speed of light) and $T$. Consider that the separation $S$ between the Solar System and the mirror increases only due to the expansion of the universe according to the law $S=s\cdot e^{H_0t}$, where $s$ is the initial separation. You may use $e^x\approx1+x$ for $x\ll1$, if necessary and assume that light travels a distance $ct$ in time $t$ in this expanding universe.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Imagine that such a mirror is located in the vicinity of the star Vega (which also features on the logo of the 1st GeCAA). Vega was the first star outside the Solar System to be photographed and one of the first stars whose parallax ($p=0.125''$) was accurately measured in 1840 by G. W. von Struve. Estimate the total duration of this $H_0$ measurement experiment. Give the answer in years.

solution.statement:
**(a)** Let $t_1$ be the time taken by the light beam from the Solar System to the mirror, let $t_2$ be the time taken by the beam from the mirror to the Solar System and $T$ the total time to go back and forth. As a first order approximation, we will take distance travelled by the photon in each part as an average of the initial and final distance. Therefore, equating the kinematics of the situation, we have:

$$S_1=\frac{D+De^{H_0t_1}}2=\frac{D(1+e^{H_0t_1})}2=ct_1,$$

$$S_2=\frac{S_1+S_1e^{H_0t_2}}2=\frac{S_1(1+e^{H_0t_2})}2=ct_2.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\frac D4(1+e^{H_0t_1})(1+e^{H_0t_2})\approx\frac D4(2+H_0t_1)(2+H_0t_2)\approx\frac D4[4+2H_0(t_1+t_2)],$$

$$S_2=D\left(1+\frac12H_0T\right).\qquad[1.5]$$

From the first equation, we also find:

$$S_1=ct_1=\frac{D(1+e^{H_0t_1})}2,$$

$$ct_1=D\left(1+\frac12H_0t_1\right),\qquad\therefore t_1=\frac D{c-\frac12DH_0},$$

$$S_1=ct_1=\frac{2Dc}{2c-DH_0}.\qquad[1.5]$$

Similarly, $S_2=2S_1c/(2c-S_1H_0)$. **[0.5]** Joining the expressions found, we obtain:

$$S_2=D\left(1+\frac12H_0T\right)=\frac{2S_1c}{2c-S_1H_0},$$

$$D\left(1+\frac12H_0T\right)=\frac{\frac{4Dc^2}{2c-DH_0}}{2c-\frac{2Dc}{2c-DH_0}\cdot H_0},$$

$$1+\frac12H_0T=\frac{2c}{2c-DH_0-DH_0}=\frac c{c-DH_0},$$

$$c=\left(1+\frac12H_0T\right)(c-DH_0)=c-DH_0+\frac12cH_0T-\frac12DH_0^2T,$$

$$0=\frac{H_0}2(cT-2D-DH_0T),\qquad H_0=\frac{cT-2D}{DT}.\qquad[2.5]$$

**Alternative solution**

First note that the time taken for the laser beam to travel to the mirror and back again is equal to the time taken for the laser beam to travel a distance of $2D$ (measured at $t=0$) in a straight line. **[2.0]** The co-moving distance the beam has to cover is the same in both scenarios. We then equate the distance travelled by the light with the amount by which the space has expanded in that time.

In time $t$, the space has expanded by a factor of $\exp(H_0t)$, to first order we can linearise this to $1+H_0t$. This means that the beam, on average, travels through space that’s stretched out by a factor of $1+H_0T/2$. Thus, **[2.5]**

$$cT=2D\left(1+\frac{H_0T}2\right),\qquad H_0=\frac{cT-2D}{DT}.\qquad[2.5]$$

**Better approximation (not required in the exam)**

In reality, the light does not travel a distance of $ct$ in this expanding universe. To find the exact expression, consider a time differential $dt$ time $t$ after the beam was emitted. In this small time interval, the beam travels a distance of $c\,dt$. Because the space is stretched out, the travelled distance corresponds to a smaller segment of space at $t=0$, smaller by a factor of $\exp(H_0t)$. The distance spanned at $t=0$ is then

$$dr=\exp(-H_0t)c\,dt.$$

We integrate this from $t=0$ to $t=T$:

$$\int_0^{2D}dr=c\int_0^T\exp(-H_0t)\,dt,\qquad2D=\frac c{H_0}(1-\exp(-H_0T)).$$

The result so far is accurate within the constraints of the model, but it’s not analytically solvable for $H_0$. To get an estimate, we can approximate the right hand side to

$$2D=\frac c{H_0}\left(1-1+H_0T-\frac{(H_0T)^2}2\right)=cT-\frac{cH_0T^2}2.$$

Expressing $H_0$, we get

$$H_0=\frac2{cT^2}(cT-2D).$$

The difference between this answer and the initial estimate is $2D/cT$ which is almost unitary.

**(b)** From the $H_0$ expression found in the previous item, we find the travel time

$$T=\frac{2D}{c-DH_0}.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\left(\frac c{2D}-\frac{H_0}2\right)^{-1}\approx\left(\frac c{2D}\right)^{-1}=\frac{2D}c.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$T=\frac{2\times8\times3.086\times10^{16}}{3\times10^8}=1.65\times10^9\ \mathrm s,\qquad T\approx52.2\ \mathrm{yr}.\qquad[1.0]$$

> **Source note:** The primary bilingual question explicitly assumes light travels $ct$ in time $t$; this sentence is omitted from the English key’s reprinted question. The key itself labels the complete final derivation “Better approximation (not required in the exam)”. Both the requested model and this native supplementary approximation are retained.

problems.title: Light Curves
problems.statement:
The light curve A shown below, shows a fictional edge-on eclipsing binary system containing stars X (radius $r_X$, luminosity $L_X$) and Y (radius $r_Y$, luminosity $L_Y$). Assume that star X is brighter, but star Y is hotter.

[[figure:p4-fig1]]

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Which of the two stars is more likely to be on the main sequence? (Choose “X” or “Y”)

parts.label: b.i)
parts.statement: Based on light curve A, estimate $r_X/r_Y$, the ratio of the radii of the two stars;

parts.label: b.ii)
parts.statement: Based on light curve A, estimate $L_X/L_Y$, the ratio of the luminosities of the two stars.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
For light curves B to F, in each case only one parameter of the binary system has been changed from the case in light curve A. For each case, choose the description from the following list that best corresponds to the change (write the appropriate number in the answer sheet).

1. Star X increased in size.
2. Star X increased in luminosity.
3. Star X decreased in size.
4. Star X decreased in luminosity.
5. Star Y increased in size.
6. Star Y increased in luminosity.
7. Star Y decreased in size.
8. Star Y decreased in luminosity.
9. Star X is a variable star.
10. Star Y is a variable star.
11. The inclination of the system relative to the Earth has changed.
12. The distance of the system from the Earth has decreased.
13. The distance of the system from the Earth has increased.
14. The orbital period of the system increased.
15. The orbital period of the system decreased.

[[figure:p4-fig2]]

answer.value: B: (cxi); C: (cxii); D: (cix); E: (cxv); F: (cx), as printed in the official key.

figures.alt: Entire light curve A, all deep and shallow eclipses, graph boundary/grid, Light curve A/Flux/Time labels and all native ticks.
figures.caption: Рис. 1: Кривая блеска A: зависимость освещённости от времени (в сутках)

figures.alt: All five complete native light curves B,C,D,E,F in original composite arrangement, complete graph frames/gridlines/flux and time axes/ticks, all dips and variable-star fluctuations.
figures.caption: Рис. 2: Кривые блеска B–F

solution.statement:
**(a)** As “Y” is smaller, yet hotter, it must be on the main sequence. **[1.0]**

**(b) (I)** For this we have to measure the total duration of eclipse and compare it with bottom flat part (total eclipse phase) in the lightcurve. Total eclipse time should be $(1.25\pm0.10)$ days, flat period of eclipse $(0.25\pm0.05)$ days. **[1.0]**

$$\frac{r_X+r_Y}{r_X-r_Y}=\frac{1.25\pm0.10}{0.25\pm0.05}=5.0\pm1.5,$$

$$\therefore\frac{r_X}{r_Y}=\frac{5+1}{5-1}=1.5\pm0.2.\qquad[1.0]$$

**(II)** Because star Y is hotter, star Y will be brighter than a part of star X with the same area. Thus, the deeper dip in the light curve is due to star Y passing behind star X. Thus, the flux from star X must be $10\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. As the combined flux is $16\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$, the flux of star Y is $6\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. Thus

$$\frac{L_X}{L_Y}=\frac{10\times10^{-12}}{6\times10^{-12}}=1.67.\qquad[2.0]$$

**(c)**

- **Light Curve B:** We see that the dips in brightness both become shallower and have become rounded at the bottom, while the maximum brightness is still $16\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. If radius of one of the stars had changed (rounded bottom), then we would expect that total eclipse period to also change. But that has not happened. Brightening of star X can explain shallower dip but not rounded trough. This means that the stars no longer fully eclipse each other. Hence, **(cxi): The inclination of the system relative to the Earth has changed. [4.0]**
- **Light Curve C:** The y-axis shows that the overall flux has increased. Since flux of both the stars has gone up by the same factor and there is no substantial change in the profile of eclipse, **(cxii): The distance of the system from the Earth has decreased. [4.0]**
- **Light Curve D:** The regular fluctuations in brightness indicate the one components of the system is a variable star. Since the fluctuations persist through all the dips in flux, this indicates that the variable star is never completely eclipsed. Therefore, **(cix): Star X is a variable star. [3.0]**
- **Light Curve E:** The overall flux and dips in the flux are the same size, but occur much more frequently. This means that **(cxv): The orbital period of the system decreased. [2.0]**
- **Light Curve F:** The regular fluctuations again indicate that one of the components of the system is a variable star. During the primary eclipse, light curve is perfectly flat. This can only occur if, **(cx): star Y is a variable star. [2.0]**

> **Source note:** The primary bilingual question uses options 1–15 and subparts b.i/b.ii; the English key’s reprint uses Roman (i)–(xv) and b(I)/(II), and asks for the appropriate Roman numeral. Its solution prints the c-prefixed references above. Their description correspondence to the primary question is B: 11, C: 12, D: 9, E: 15, F: 10. All repeated A–F graphs on key pages 8–9 were inspected and correspond to the native question graphs retained here. The answer sheet mentioned in the question/key was not obtained.

problems.title: HII region
problems.statement:
Luminous Blue Variables (LBV) are massive, unstable, supergiant stars that can undergo episodes of very strong mass loss, due to an instability in their atmospheres. After such an event, a dense nebula is formed around the star. LBV are also very hot stars and produce a large amount of high-energy photons that are able to ionise hydrogen atoms ($E_{\mathrm{ph}}>h\nu_0=13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$) creating a roughly spherical region of ionized hydrogen (HII region).

In this problem, we consider a static, homogeneous, pure hydrogen nebula with a concentration of $n_H=10^8/\mathrm{m^3}$ and temperature $T_{\mathrm{HII}}=10^4\ \mathrm K$, ionized by photons from a single LBV star with a stable rate of ionizing photons $Q=10^{49}\ \mathrm{ph/s}$. Assume that each photon can ionise only one hydrogen atom.

At a particular location within an HII region, the rate of photoionization is balanced by the rate of recombination per unit volume. This sets the radius of the fully ionized region and this region is called the Stromgren sphere with the radius $R_S$.

The total number of recombinations per volume is proportional to the concentration of protons $n_p$, the concentration of electrons $n_e$ and the recombination coefficient for hydrogen $\alpha(T_{\mathrm{HII}})=10^{-19}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$. For simplification, ignore the fact that the process of recombination can also release ionising photons.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Derive an algebraic expression for the radius of the Stromgren sphere and calculate its value for the given parameters. Give the answer in parsecs.

parts.label: b)
c)
parts.statement: On what timescale do you expect the Stromgren sphere to form? Give the answer in years.

parts.label: d)
parts.statement: Radiation from an ionized hydrogen cloud (HII region) is often called free-free emission because it is produced by free electrons scattering off the ions without being captured: the electrons are free before the interaction and remain free afterwards. In this process, the electron retains most of its pre-scattering energy. An electron, while passing by a much more massive singly ionized hydrogen atom, produces a radio photon of $\nu=10\ \mathrm{GHz}$. Calculate the mean electron thermal energy in the HII region, for the given temperature of the Stromgren sphere. Is this an example of free-free emission? (answer “YES” or “NO”)

parts.label: e)
parts.statement:
Since the HII region is in local thermodynamic equilibrium, one can calculate the absorption coefficient that is proportional to the optical depth $	au_
u\propto
u^{-2.1}$ and it turns out that at sufficiently high radio frequencies, the hot plasma is nearly transparent and hence $	au_
u\ll1$. The flux density of photons has power-law spectra of the form $S_
u\propto
u^ eta$. Find $ eta$ for the radio frequencies. Write the numeric value of beta.

solution.statement:
**(a)** As the number of H-atoms undergoing ionization and recombination are balanced at $R_S$, each photon can ionize exactly one hydrogen atom and each neutral hydrogen has exactly one proton and one electron,

$$n_{\mathrm{recomb}}=n_{\mathrm{HII}}=Q,\qquad\text{and }n_e=n_p=n_H.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$n_{\mathrm{recomb}}=\alpha n_pn_eV_S,\qquad Q=\alpha n_H^2\frac{4\pi}3R_S^3.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\therefore R_S=\sqrt[3]{\frac{3Q}{4\pi\alpha n_H^2}}.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\sqrt[3]{\frac{3\times10^{49}}{4\pi\times10^{-19}\times(10^8)^2}}=1.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm m,\qquad\therefore R_S\approx4\ \mathrm{pc}.\qquad[1.0]$$

**(b)** Per one unit length distance, a typical photon will encounter $\sigma n_H$ H-atoms. Thus, the mean free path will be,

$$l_{\nu_0}=\frac1{\sigma n_H}=\frac1{\sigma10^{-21}\times10^8},\qquad l_{\nu_0}=10^{13}\ \mathrm m.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$\therefore l_{\nu_0}\approx10^{-4}R_S\ll R_S.$$

Thus, the boundary layer of the sphere is very thin as compared to its total size. Hence, “YES” this ionized nebula is very sharp-edged. **[1.0]**

**(c)** For Stromgren sphere to form, all H-atoms ($N$) inside $R_S$ need to be ionized. Thus, time $t_S$ required will be

$$N=V_Sn_H=\frac{4\pi}3R_S^3n_H.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$t_S=\frac NQ=\frac{4\pi R_S^3n_H}{3Q}.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$=\frac1{\alpha n_H}=\frac1{10^{-19}\times10^8}=10^{11}\ \mathrm s\approx3000\ \mathrm{yr}.\qquad[2.0]$$

For typical nebular densities, the main-sequence lifetime of LBV stars is much longer than this ionization time, and hence our assumption of a stationary system is justified.

**(d)** The mean electron thermal energy in a plasma of temperature $T_e=10^4\ \mathrm K$ is

$$E_e\approx k_BT_e\approx1.4\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J\approx0.9\ \mathrm{eV}.\qquad[2.0]$$

The energy of a photon is

$$E_\gamma=h\nu\approx6.6\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm J\approx4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}.\qquad[1.0]$$

As the energy of the radio photon is much much smaller than that of the electron, the answer is “Yes”. **[1.0]**

**(e)** As the plasma is nearly transparent, using the Rayleigh-Jeans law,

$$B_\nu=\frac{2k_BT_e\nu^2}{c^2}.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$S_\nu\propto B_\nu\tau_\nu=\frac{2k_BT_e\nu^2}{c^2}\tau_\nu,\qquad S_\nu\propto\nu^2\cdot\nu^{-2.1},\qquad\therefore S_\nu\propto\nu^{-0.1}.\qquad[3.0]$$

> **Source note:** The key’s numeric mean-free-path substitution prints an extra $\sigma$ in the denominator before $10^{-21}$. This printed form is retained alongside its native result; it has not been silently corrected.

problems.title: Occultation of a X-ray Source
problems.statement:
Consider a satellite observing X-ray sources, while orbiting the Earth in the equatorial plane with orbital radius $r$, and orbital time period $P$. Assume that this satellite is pointed in one fixed direction in space for a given length of time. Take the radius of the Earth as $R$.

When the satellite moves ‘behind’ the Earth in its orbit, the X-ray source is ‘occulted’ and the measured X-ray flux from the source drops to zero. However, due to Earth’s atmosphere, this drop is gradual. If the line of sight to the source passes through the atmosphere, the extent of the attenuation depends on the air-mass (i.e. length of air column) along the line of sight.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Let us assume that the satellite is pointing towards a fixed source at $0^\circ$ declination. We consider that the source is occulted when 50% of the light coming from the source gets attenuated due to the atmosphere. Let us say that this happens when the minimum height of the line of sight from the surface of the Earth is $h$. If $\theta_0$ is the angle between the direction of the source and the direction of the Earth, as measured from the spacecraft, find an expression for $\theta_0$.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: The time duration $\Delta t$ between the source getting attenuated from 90% of the pre-occultation flux to 10% is defined as the ‘occultation time’ for the source. Assume the flux attenuates to 90% when the minimum height of the line of sight $(h+0.5\Delta h)$ and similarly the flux attenuates to 10% at $(h-0.5\Delta h)$, where $\Delta h\ll R$. Find the expression for $\Delta t$ in terms of $r$, $P$, $\Delta h$ and $\theta_0$.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: If the satellite was pointing towards a source at an arbitrary declination $\beta$ instead (where $\beta$ is not too large), what will be the expression for $\Delta t$?

problems.statementAfterParts: Note: If the satellite was not in the equatorial plane, then the problem could have been simply rephrased by assuming the satellite’s orbital plane to be the equatorial plane. In that case, $\beta$ becomes ‘relative declination’.

solution.statement:
**(a)** The solution for first part is obvious from the figure below.

[[figure:p6-sol-fig1]]

$$\sin\theta_0=\left(\frac{R+h}r\right),\qquad\therefore\theta_0=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{R+h}r\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

**(b)** Let us say the satelite has to move in the orbit by $\Delta\theta/2$ for $0.5\Delta h/2$ change in height.

$$\sin\left(\theta_0\pm\frac{\Delta\theta}2\right)=\left(\frac{R+h\pm0.5\Delta h}r\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\sin\left(\theta_0+\frac{\Delta\theta}2\right)-\sin\left(\theta_0-\frac{\Delta\theta}2\right)=\left(\frac{\Delta h}r\right),$$

$$\therefore2\cos\theta_0\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\theta}2\right)=\left(\frac{\Delta h}r\right),$$

$$2\times\frac{\Delta\theta}2\cos\theta_0=\left(\frac{\Delta h}r\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\Delta\theta=\left(\frac{\Delta h}{r\cos\theta_0}\right)=\frac{2\pi\Delta t}P.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\therefore\Delta t=\left(\frac{P\Delta h}{2\pi r\cos\theta_0}\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

**(c)** Let $\theta$ be the new angle for 50% attenuation. In the diagram below, The line of sight from the satelite (S) to the source is at minimum distance from the centre of the earth (C) at point A. The points S, C and B are in the equatorial plane with line BA normal to the equatorial plane. One also realises that the line BS is normal to the plane defined by A, B and C. **[3.0]**

[[figure:p6-sol-fig2]]

$$a=r\cos\theta,\qquad c=r\sin\theta,\qquad b=a\tan\beta,$$

$$ (R+h)^2=b^2+c^2=(r\cos\theta\tan\beta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2.\qquad[3.0]$$

$$\therefore\frac{(R+h)^2}{r^2}=\cos^2\theta\tan^2\beta+\sin^2\theta=(1-\sin^2\theta)\tan^2\beta+\sin^2\theta=\tan^2\beta+\sin^2\theta(1-\tan^2\beta),$$

$$\therefore\sin^2\theta=\left(\frac{(R+h)^2}{r^2}-\tan^2\beta\right)\left(\frac1{1-\tan^2\beta}\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

Let us say $\tan^2\beta=k$.

$$\therefore\sin\theta=\sqrt{\left(\frac{(R+h)^2}{r^2}-k\right)\left(\frac1{1-k}\right)}.$$

Using similar analysis as the previous part,

$$\Delta\theta\cos\theta=\sqrt{\frac1{1-k}}\left[\sqrt{\frac{(R+h+\frac{\Delta h}2)^2}{r^2}-k}-\sqrt{\frac{(R+h-\frac{\Delta h}2)^2}{r^2}-k}\right].\qquad[2.0]$$

$$=\sqrt{\frac1{1-k}}\left(\frac{\Delta h(R+h)}{r^2}\right)\left(\frac{(R+h)^2}{r^2}-k\right)^{-0.5}.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$=\sqrt{\frac1{1-k}\left(\frac{(R+h)^2}{r^2}-k\right)}\left(\frac{\Delta h}r\times\frac{R+h}r\right)\left(\left(\frac{R+h}r\right)^2-k\right)^{-1}.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$=\sin\theta\left(\frac{\Delta h\sin\theta_0}r\right)(\sin^2\theta_0-\tan^2\beta)^{-1},$$

$$\therefore\Delta t=\left(\frac{P\Delta h\tan\theta}{2\pi r}\right)\left(\frac{\sin\theta_0}{\sin^2\theta_0-\tan^2\beta}\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

> **Source note:** The key’s opening prose in (b) prints $0.5\Delta h/2$, while the immediately following formula uses $0.5\Delta h$. The extra divisor in the printed prose is retained; the derivation is transcribed as printed.

problems.title: Radiant of a Meteor Shower
problems.statement: A stargazer in Chiayi, Chinese Taipei ($23.5^\circ\ \mathrm N$, $120.4^\circ\ \mathrm E$, GMT+8) saw two meteors streaking through the sky at 21:00 (Chinese Taipei time) on 25th September 2020. One of the meteors originated directly above the northern horizon at $15^\circ$ altitude and streaked to meet the horizon exactly due east. The second meteor originated at an altitude of $23.5^\circ$ and an azimuth of $210^\circ$ and ended at an altitude of $75^\circ$ and an azimuth of $255^\circ$.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: What is the Local Sidereal Time (LST) at the time of observation?

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Find the alt-az coordinates of the apparent radiant of the two meteors.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: Find the equatorial coordinates of the apparent radiant.

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
Which of the following constellations is closest to the radiant?

- Crux
- Dorado
- Pavo
- Tucana
- Triangulum Australes

problems.statementAfterParts:
Notes:

- Azimuths are measured from the North ($0^\circ$) towards the East.
- The Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST) at 00:00 UT on 1st January 2020 is $6^{\mathrm h}\,40^{\mathrm m}\,30^{\mathrm s}$.

solution.statement:
> **Source edition note:** The English key’s reprinted first meteor description is: “One of the meteors appeared at horizon exactly due west and streaked to a point at 15° altitude directly above the northern horizon.” The primary bilingual question instead gives 15° above north to the eastern horizon. Both worked methods below use the latter endpoint coordinates. The key’s (d) additionally says to choose one constellation and write the same name in the answer box; that answer box/sheet was not obtained.

**(a) Step 1: Determine the GST at the time of observation.** Let us denote the GST on at 00:00 UT on 1st January 2020 as $\mathrm{GST}_0$. Total 268 days have elapsed since start of the year till $0^{\mathrm h}$ UT on 25 September. **[1.0]**

At 21:00 for GMT+8 timezone, UT will be $21^{\mathrm h}-8^{\mathrm h}=13^{\mathrm h}$. Hence,

$$\mathrm{GST}=\mathrm{GST}_0+\Delta t=6^{\mathrm h}40^{\mathrm m}30^{\mathrm s}+\frac{268\times24}{365.2422}+\frac{13\times24}{23.9344},$$

$$\approx6^{\mathrm h}40^{\mathrm m}30^{\mathrm s}+17^{\mathrm h}36^{\mathrm m}36^{\mathrm s}+13^{\mathrm h}2^{\mathrm m}8^{\mathrm s}=37^{\mathrm h}19^{\mathrm m}14^{\mathrm s}=13^{\mathrm h}19^{\mathrm m}14^{\mathrm s}.\qquad[3.0]$$

As longitude of observer is $120.4^\circ$, the LST of observation is,

$$\mathrm{LST}=\mathrm{GST}+24^{\mathrm h}\times\frac{120.4^\circ}{360^\circ}=13^{\mathrm h}19^{\mathrm m}14^{\mathrm s}+8^{\mathrm h}1^{\mathrm m}36^{\mathrm s}=21^{\mathrm h}20^{\mathrm m}50^{\mathrm s}.\qquad[2.0]$$

**(b) For horizontal coordinates**

[[figure:p7-sol-fig1]]

**[1.0]** The spherical triangle has the radiant, initial position and final position of the $i$-th meteor to be $(A,a)$, $(A_i,a_i)$ and $(A'_i,a'_i)$, where $a$ and $A$ denotes the altitude and azimuth respectively. Using the four-parts (cotangent) equation on the left and right triangles, we have, for both meteors:

$$\cos(90-a_i)\cos(A'_i-A_i)=\sin(90-a_i)\cot(90-a'_i)-\sin(A'_i-A_i)\cot\theta,$$

$$\therefore\sin a_i\cos(A'_i-A_i)=\cos a_i\tan a'_i-\sin(A'_i-A_i)\cot\theta.$$

Similarly,

$$\cos(90-a_i)\cos(A_i-A)=\sin(90-a_i)\cot(90-a)-\sin(A_i-A)\cot(180-\theta),$$

$$\therefore\sin a_i\cos(A_i-A)=\cos a_i\tan a+\sin(A_i-A)\cot\theta.\qquad[2.0]$$

We can then eliminate $\cot\theta$ to yield:

$$\frac{\sin a_i\cos(A_i-A)}{\sin(A_i-A)}-\frac{\cos a_i\tan a}{\sin(A_i-A)}=\frac{\cos a_i\tan a'_i}{\sin(A'_i-A_i)}-\frac{\sin a_i\cos(A'_i-A_i)}{\sin(A'_i-A_i)}=\cot\theta.$$

Multiplying the whole equation by $\sin(A'_i-A_i)\sin(A_i-A)/\cos a_i$,

$$\begin{aligned}\tan a_i\cos(A_i-A)\sin(A'_i-A)&\quad\tan a'_i\sin(A_i-A)\\-\tan a\sin(A'_i-A)&=-\tan a_i\cos(A'_i-A_i)\sin(A_i-A),\end{aligned}$$

$$\tan a_i\sin[(A'_i-A_i)+(A_i-A)]=\tan a'_i\sin(A_i-A)+\tan a\sin(A'_i-A_i),$$

$$\tan a_i\sin(A'_i-A)=\tan a'_i\sin(A_i-A)+\tan a\sin(A'_i-A_i).\qquad[3.0]$$

Plugging in $i=1,2$, and eliminating $\tan a$ by division, we have

$$\frac{\tan a_1\sin(A'_1-A)-\tan a'_1\sin(A_1-A)}{\tan a_2\sin(A'_2-A)-\tan a'_2\sin(A_2-A)}=\frac{\sin(A'_1-A_1)}{\sin(A'_2-A_2)}\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{def}}=}k,$$

where $k$ is the RHS defined above (which is a known value). Expanding the equation above and dividing by $\cos A$, gathering terms of $\tan A$, we get

$$\tan A=\frac{\tan a_1\sin A'_1-\tan a'_1\sin A_1-k\tan a_2\sin A'_2+k\tan a'_2\sin A_2}{\tan a_1\cos A'_1-\tan a'_1\cos A_1-k\tan a_2\cos A'_2+k\tan a'_2\cos A_2}.\qquad[2.0]$$

And

$$\tan a=\frac{\tan a_1\sin(A'_1-A)-\tan a'_1\sin(A_1-A)}{\sin(A'_1-A_1)}.$$

Plugging in the respective values from the question,

| | Azimuth | Altitude |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial first meteor | $A_1=0^\circ$ | $a_1=15^\circ$ |
| Final first meteor | $A'_1=90^\circ$ | $a'_1=0^\circ$ |
| Initial second meteor | $A_2=210^\circ$ | $a_2=23.5^\circ$ |
| Final second meteor | $A'_2=255^\circ$ | $a'_2=75^\circ$ |

We get

$$k=\frac{\sin(A'_1-A_1)}{\sin(A'_2-A_2)}=\frac{\sin90^\circ}{\sin15^\circ},\qquad k=1.414,$$

$$\begin{aligned}\tan a_1\sin A'_1&=0.268,&\tan a'_1\sin A_1&=0,\\k\tan a_2\sin A'_2&=-0.594,&k\tan a'_2\sin A_2&=-2.639,\\\tan a_1\cos A'_1&=0,&\tan a'_1\cos A_1&=0,\\k\tan a_2\cos A'_2&=-0.159,&k\tan a'_2\cos A_2&=-4.571.\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\tan A=\frac{0.268-0+0.594-2.639}{0-0+0.159-4.571}=0.403,$$

$$\therefore A=21.94^\circ,\qquad\mathrm{OR}\quad A=201.94^\circ.\qquad[4.0]$$

However, the student should realize that for $A=21.94^\circ$, the radiant is in the path of the first meteor, which is unrealistic. Hence, it is more likely that the azimuth takes the second value. **[1.0]** Plugging in for the altitude, we find the coordinate of the radiant to be

$$\tan a_1\sin(A'_1-A)=-0.249,\quad\tan a'_1\sin(A_1-A)=0,\quad\sin(A'_1-A_1)=1,$$

$$\therefore\tan a=(-0.2485-0)/1=-0.2485,\qquad a=-13.96^\circ.\qquad[2.0]$$

As the meteor track origin and end points are rounded to integer degrees, the horizontal coordinates of the radiant will be

$$ (A,a)=(202^\circ,-14^\circ).\qquad[1.0]$$

**Alternative solution**

In the vector representation, let the starting and final locations of the meteroids be $\vec u_i$ and $\vec v_i$ respectively. For the subsequent calculations, the vectors are most conveniently represented in Cartesian coordinates. Letting the $x$-axis point east, $y$-axis north, and $z$-axis towards the zenith, we have

$$\vec u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)=(\cos a\sin A,\cos a\cos A,\sin a).\tag{1}$$

For a generic vector $\vec u$ with azimuth $A$ and altitude $a$. We can therefore compute

$$\vec u_1=(\cos15^\circ\sin0^\circ,\cos15^\circ\cos0^\circ,\sin15^\circ)=(0,0.9659,0.2588),$$

$$\vec u_2=(\cos23.5^\circ\sin210^\circ,\cos23.5^\circ\cos210^\circ,\sin23.5^\circ)=(-0.4585,-0.7942,0.3988),$$

$$\vec v_1=(\cos0^\circ\sin90^\circ,\cos0^\circ\cos90^\circ,\sin0^\circ)=(1,0,0),$$

$$\vec v_2=(\cos75^\circ\sin255^\circ,\cos75^\circ\cos255^\circ,\sin75^\circ)=(-0.25,-0.0670,0.9659).\qquad[3.0]$$

The meteors move along great arcs, and the two intersections of the great arcs correspond to the two possible locations of the radiant. A great arc is uniquely defined by its normal vector, denote it with $\vec n_i$. The normal vector is conveniently calculated through the cross product of the starting and final position, $\vec n_i=\vec u_i\times\vec v_i$. The cross product can be calculated via the determinant of the following matrix

$$\vec u_i\times\vec v_i=\begin{vmatrix}i&j&k\\u_{ix}&u_{iy}&u_{iz}\\v_{ix}&v_{iy}&v_{iz}\end{vmatrix}=(u_{iy}v_{iz}-u_{iz}v_{iy},u_{iz}v_{ix}-u_{ix}v_{iz},u_{ix}v_{iy}-u_{iy}v_{ix}).\qquad[4.0]$$

This yields

$$\vec n_1=(0,0.2588,-0.9659),\qquad\vec n_2=(-0.7404,0.3432,-0.1678).\qquad[1.0]$$

Every point on the great circle $i$ is perpendicular to $\vec n_i$. This means that the intersections of the two great circles are perpendicular to both $\vec n_1$ and $\vec n_2$. The vector parallel to the intersections can therefore be calculated by the cross product of $\vec n_1$ and $\vec n_2$. Let the vector corresponding to the intersection be $\vec m$. Then

$$\vec m=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2\quad[3.0]\qquad=(0.3626,0.9002,0.2412).\quad[1.0]$$

Now all that’s left is to calculate the azimuth and altitude corresponding to $\vec m$. Note that $-\vec m$ is also an intersection. The equations for the altitude and azimuth can be reverse-engineered from equation (1):

$$a=\arctan\left(\frac z{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right),\qquad A=\arctan\left(\frac xy\right).\qquad[1.0]$$

One has to take care that the arctans are signed. This gives the final values of the intersection points to be

$$ (A,a)=(22^\circ,14^\circ)\quad\text{and}\quad(A,a)=(202^\circ,-14^\circ).\qquad[2.0]$$

As in the first solution, the $A=22^\circ$ solution can be eliminated due to it being on the path of the first meteor This gives the final answer of

$$ (A,a)=(202^\circ,-14^\circ).\qquad[1.0]$$

**(c)** Now, it is easy to convert the horizontal coordinates of the radiant to equatorial coordinates.

[[figure:p7-sol-fig2]]

**[1.0]** Using the cosine rule:

$$\sin\delta=\sin\varphi\sin a+\cos\varphi\cos a\cos A,$$

$$=\sin(23.5^\circ)\sin(-13.4^\circ)+\cos(23.5^\circ)\cos(-13.96^\circ)\cos(201.94^\circ)=-0.9217,$$

$$\therefore\delta=-67.2^\circ.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$\cos H=\frac{\sin a-\sin\delta\sin\varphi}{\cos\varphi\cos\delta}=\frac{\sin(-13.4^\circ)-\sin(-67.2^\circ)\sin(23.5^\circ)}{\cos(23.5^\circ)\cos(-67.2^\circ)}=0.3551,$$

$$\therefore H=4^{\mathrm h}36^{\mathrm m}47^{\mathrm s}.\qquad[1.5]$$

From the relationship between the LST and the Hour Angle ($H=\mathrm{LST}-\alpha$), we get the equatorial coordinates of the radiant to be

$$\alpha=21^{\mathrm h}20^{\mathrm m}50^{\mathrm s}-4^{\mathrm h}36^{\mathrm m}47^{\mathrm s}=16^{\mathrm h}44^{\mathrm m}3^{\mathrm s}.\qquad[1.5]$$

Thus, the equatorial coordinates of the radiant are,

$$ (\alpha,\delta)=(16^{\mathrm h}44^{\mathrm m},-67.2^\circ).$$

**(d)** Triangulum Australes **[2.0]**

> **Source note:** The native cotangent derivation’s intermediate multiplied line prints $\sin(A'_i-A)$ where the preceding multiplier is $\sin(A'_i-A_i)$, and its first line has the right-hand term on a separate row without a printed equality. That arrangement is retained in the aligned transcription. The numeric $k$ substitution prints $\sin15^\circ$ in the denominator, followed by $k=1.414$, although the listed second azimuth difference is $45^\circ$. The equatorial substitution prints $-13.4^\circ$ as well as $-13.96^\circ$. All printed forms, numerical values, constellation spelling and marking criteria are retained.

problems.title: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot
problems.statement:
In the following problem, the fluid mechanics of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot (GRS) is studied based on the velocity field data. The diagram on the last page shows a map of relative velocity for GRS and the surrounding region. The arrows are oriented and scaled as per the directions and magnitudes of winds at different points.

Due to the combined effects of gravity and rotation, Jupiter is slightly flattened at its poles. The equation of a spheroid approximating for the shape of Jupiter can be stated as:

$$\frac{x^2+y^2}{R_e^2}+\frac{z^2}{R_p^2}=1,$$

where $R_e=7.15\times10^7\ \mathrm m$ is the equatorial radius of Jupiter, and $R_p=6.69\times10^7\ \mathrm m$ the polar radius. The radii of curvature of this spheroid in any direction can be calculated by the following equations ($\varepsilon=R_e/R_p$):

$$r(\varphi)=R_e\left(1+\varepsilon^{-2}\tan^2\varphi\right)^{-1/2},$$

$$R(\varphi)=R_e\varepsilon^{-2}\left(\frac{r(\varphi)}{R_e\cos\varphi}\right)^3.$$

where $r(\varphi)$ and $R(\varphi)$ are the zonal (aka in the zone of a particular latitude) and meridional (aka longitudinal) radii of curvature, respectively, as a function of planetographic latitude $\varphi$. The sidereal rotation period of Jupiter is $P=3.57\times10^4\ \mathrm s$.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Calculate the zonal and meridional radii values ($\bar r$ and $\bar R$ respectively) at the location of the centre of the GRS. Write numeric answer in km.

answer.value: $\bar r=6.77\times10^7\ \mathrm m$, $\bar R=6.40\times10^7\ \mathrm m$ (key’s printed units).

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Estimate the eccentricity of the GRS.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement:
‘Vorticity’ at any point is a measure of local spinning of the fluid as measured by an observer situated in the reference frame of the fluid. Mathematically, it is calculated as ‘curl’ (vector derivative product) of the velocity field. In this case, the average relative vorticity may be estimated by the equation:

$$\xi=\frac{V_wL_{\mathrm{GRS}}}{A_{\mathrm{GRS}}},$$

where $V_w$ is the maximum value of winds as per the velocity field, $L_{\mathrm{GRS}}$ is the length of the circumference of the GRS and $A_{\mathrm{GRS}}$ is the area of the GRS. Estimate average relative vorticity of the GRS. Give the answer in SI units.

Hint: The circumference of an ellipse is well approximated by an average of circumferences of the corresponding auxiliary and minor circles.

parts.label: d)
parts.statement:
Find the absolute vorticity $\xi_a=\xi+f$ by adding the Coriolis parameter

$$f=2\Omega\sin\varphi,$$

where $\Omega$ is the angular velocity of the Jupiter (due to axial rotation) and $\varphi$ is the appropriate latitude. Give the answer in SI units.

parts.label: e)
parts.statement: If the absolute vorticity has the same sign as the latitude, we call the storm a ‘cyclonic storm’. If they have opposite signs, the system is ‘anticyclonic’. Is the GRS cyclonic or anticyclonic?

parts.label: f)
parts.statement: Imagine that the GRS moves to another latitude $\varphi_1$, where the absolute vorticity changes the sign (changes from anti-cyclonic to cyclonic or vice versa). Assuming minimum possible displacement of the GRS, at what value of $\varphi_1$ do we expect this change? Give the answer in degrees, rounded to nearest integer. In your analysis, assume that the GRS at the new location would occupy the same angular span in latitude, as well as have the same wind velocities and eccentricity as the original.

solution.statement:
**(a)** From the figure, the centre of GRS lies at $\varphi=-20.0^\circ$. **[1.0]**

$$\epsilon=\frac{R_e}{R_p}=\frac{7.15}{6.69}=1.069.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\bar r=r(-20^\circ)=R_e(1+\epsilon^{-2}\tan^2\varphi)^{-1/2}=7.15\times10^7\times\left(1+(1.0688)^{-2}\tan^2(-20^\circ)\right)^{-1/2},$$

$$\bar r=6.77\times10^7\ \mathrm m.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$\bar R=R(-20^\circ)=R_e\epsilon^{-2}\left(\frac{r(\varphi)}{R_e\cos\varphi}\right)^3=7.15\times10^7\times(1.0688)^{-2}\left(\frac{r(-20^\circ)}{7.15\times10^7\times\cos(-20^\circ)}\right)^3,$$

$$\bar R=6.40\times10^7\ \mathrm m.\qquad[1.0]$$

**(b)** We use the figure to estimate size major and minor axis of the GRS and hence estimate the eccentricity.

$$a=\bar r\theta_{\mathrm{long}}=6.77\times10^7\times\frac{8.2^\circ\times\pi}{180^\circ},\qquad a=9.69\times10^6\ \mathrm m.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$b=\bar R\theta_{\mathrm{lat}}=6.40\times10^7\times\frac{4.3^\circ\times\pi}{180^\circ},\qquad b=4.80\times10^6\ \mathrm m.\qquad[2.0]$$

$$e_{\mathrm{GRS}}=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac ba\right)^2}=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{4.8}{9.7}\right)^2},\qquad e_{\mathrm{GRS}}\approx0.87.\qquad[1.0]$$

**(c)** The maximum value of wind velocity ($V_w$) is about 120 m/s. **[1.0]**

$$A_{\mathrm{GRS}}=\pi ab.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$L_{\mathrm{GRS}}\approx\frac{2\pi a+2\pi b}2=\pi a(1+\sqrt{1-e^2}).\qquad[2.0]$$

$$\therefore\xi=\frac{V_wL_{\mathrm{GRS}}}{A_{\mathrm{GRS}}}=\frac{V_w\pi a(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})}{\pi ab}=\frac{120\times(1+\sqrt{1-0.87^2})}{4.8\times10^6},$$

$$\xi\approx3.7\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.\qquad[2.0]$$

**(d)** The absolute vorticity will be given by

$$\xi_a=\xi+2\Omega\sin\varphi=\xi+\frac{2\times2\times\pi\sin(-20^\circ)}P=3.7\times10^{-5}+\frac{4\pi\sin(-20^\circ)}{3.57\times10^4},$$

$$=3.7\times10^{-5}-1.2\times10^{-4},\qquad\xi_a=-8.3\times10^{-5}.\qquad[2.0]$$

**(e)** The GRS is a cyclonic system. **[1.0]**

**(f)** For this, we have to write $\xi_a$ as a function of $\varphi$ and then find root of the function closest to the current latitude.

$$\xi_a=0=\xi+2\Omega\sin\varphi.\qquad[1.0]$$

$$0=\frac{V_w(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})}b+2\Omega\sin\varphi_1,$$

$$0=\frac{V_w(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})}{\bar R_1\theta_{\mathrm{lat}}}+2\Omega\sin\varphi_1,$$

$$0=\frac{V_w\epsilon^2R_e^2(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})\cos^3\varphi}{\theta_{\mathrm{lat}}r^3(\varphi_1)}+2\Omega\sin\varphi_1,$$

$$0=\frac{V_w\epsilon^2R_e^2(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})\cos^3\varphi_1}{\theta_{\mathrm{lat}}\left(R_e(1+\epsilon^{-2}\tan^2\varphi_1)^{-1/2}\right)^3}+2\Omega\sin\varphi_1.\qquad[3.0]$$

$$0=\left(\frac{V_w\epsilon^2(1+\sqrt{1-e^2})}{\theta_{\mathrm{lat}}R_e}\right)\left(\cos\varphi_1\sqrt{1+\epsilon^{-2}\tan^2\varphi_1}\right)^3+2\Omega\sin\varphi_1,$$

$$-3.520\times10^{-4}\sin\varphi_1=3.81\times10^{-5}\times\left(1-(1-\epsilon^{-2})\sin^2\varphi_1\right)^{3/2},$$

$$35.2^2\sin^2\varphi_1=3.81^2\times\left(1-(1-\epsilon^{-2})\sin^2\varphi_1\right)^3.$$

Let us define $\sin^2\varphi_1=x$.

$$\therefore x=0.01172(1-0.1245x)^3.\qquad[4.0]$$

Iterating over $x$, with starting value as $x_0=\sin^2(-20^\circ)=0.11698$,

| $x_0$ | $x_1$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.11698 | 0.01121 |
| 0.01121 | 0.01167 |
| 0.01167 | 0.01167 |

**[2.0]** Thus,

$$\varphi_1=-\sin^{-1}(\sqrt{0.01167}),\qquad\varphi_1=-6.2^\circ\approx-6^\circ.\qquad[2.0]$$

An alternative solution is to try to find this using the plotting method, but one needs to make sure the result is obtained to the equivalent precision.
